chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, altogether from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about the lost one (al-mafqud), so he (peace be upon him) said: 'If it is known that he is in a land, she waits for him forever until his death comes to her or his divorce comes to her. And if it is not known where he is from the whole of the earth, and no letter comes from him, nor any news, then she goes to the Imam (peace be upon him). He orders her to wait for four years, and he seeks him in the earth. So if no trace is found for him until four years pass, he orders her to observe the waiting period (iddah) of four months and ten days, then she becomes permissible for men. So if her husband comes after her waiting period has expired, it is not for him any reversion to her. And if he comes while she is in her waiting period of four months and ten days, then he is in control with reverting back to her.'

key_terms.الْإِمَام: The Imam (the religious authority who issues the ruling)
key_terms.الْمَفْقُود: The lost one (a specific legal status for a missing person in Islamic jurisprudence)
key_terms.رَجْعَةٌ: Reversion (the husband's right to take back his wife during the waiting period without a new contract)
key_terms.عِدَّة: Waiting period (period a woman must observe after divorce or death before remarrying)

ai.seo_question: What is the waiting period for a wife whose husband is missing and his location is unknown?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the jurisprudential distinction for 'al-mafqud' (the missing person) based on the certainty of location, a key topic in Shia fiqh regarding marital status. It highlights the Imam's authority to mandate a four-year search period before the wife observes the standard 'iddah of four months and ten days, ensuring legal clarity for remarriage. The ruling emphasizes the finality of remarriage if the husband returns after the 'iddah concludes, reflecting the principle of 'istishab' (presumption of continuity) in Shia legal theory.
